extraction.name: FLEURS: Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech
extraction.description: FLEURS is an n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language. FLEURS can be used for a variety of speech tasks, including Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation and Retrieval. The dataset contains natural human speech and high quality transcripts for each language with strong quality control.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Min Ma, Simran Khanuja, Yu Zhang, Vera Axelrod, Siddharth Dalmia, Jason Riesa, Clara Rivera, Ankur Bapna
extraction.publisher: Meta AI Research, Google Research, Carnegie Mellon University
extraction.inLanguage: 102 languages including Western European, Eastern European, Central-Asian/Middle-East/North-African, Sub-Saharan African, South Asian, South-East Asian, and CJK languages
extraction.citeAs: Conneau, A., Ma, M., Khanuja, S., Zhang, Y., Axelrod, V., Dalmia, S., Riesa, J., Rivera, C., & Bapna, A. (2022). FLEURS: Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech. arXiv:2205.12446v1 [cs.CL].
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The data collection process starts with the FLoRes-101 dataset, which contains 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia translated into 101 languages by human translators. The dev and devtest sets (2009 sentences total) were used and split into new train, dev and test splits (1509, 150 and 350 sentences respectively). For each sentence in 102 languages, three recordings were collected from three different native speakers, with a sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible. Each recording was then evaluated by additional workers to assess whether the recording corresponds to the input sentence. Invalid recordings were discarded. All recordings are kept as-is without any data augmentations. The speech sampling rate is 16kHz. Data was split into train, development and test sets with disjoint speakers between train/dev and test, with a target ratio of 7:1:2. All segments are within 30 seconds.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: About 21.5% of the sentences are missing in the first version of the dataset because none of the three recordings were validated. The authors plan to fill these gaps in future versions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: FLoRes-101 dataset sentences (extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into 101 languages by human translators). The dev and devtest sets containing 2009 sentences were used as the source text.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Sentences from FLoRes-101 dev and devtest sets (2009 sentences) were split into new train, dev and test splits with 1509, 150 and 350 sentences respectively. Speakers are disjoint between train/dev and test sets. The Chinese (Simp) language was renamed to Mandarin Chinese (code 'cmn') and Chinese (Trad) to Cantonese Chinese (code 'yue').
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For textual data: NFC and FST normalization applied to each sentence, lower-casing, normalization and removal of punctuations. Words are split into characters, with token 'j' defined as word boundaries. Three versions of each sentence are provided: original raw transcript (SRC_RAW), preprocessed version (SRC_NORM), and character-based version (SRC_CHAR). A universal vocabulary of characters is adopted as the modeling and evaluation unit. For speech: recordings are kept as-is without data augmentations (e.g., SpecAugment, speed perturbation, simulated reverberation). Speech sampling rate is 16kHz.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each sentence was recorded by three different native speakers. After recording, each recording was evaluated by additional workers to assess whether the recording corresponds to the input sentence. Invalid recordings were discarded, leaving between zero and three recordings per sentence in the final dataset. Source transcripts were reused from human translators from FLoRes-101.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Invalid recordings identified by additional worker evaluation were discarded. About 21.5% of sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Up to 3 recordings per sentence (by 3 different native speakers), plus validation by additional workers
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Native speakers of each respective language, with a sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% imposed when possible
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly available via TFDS at https://tensorflow.org/datasets/catalog/xtreme_s and Huggingface at https://hf.co/datasets/google/xtreme_s. The authors plan to fill missing data gaps (approximately 21.5% of sentences) in future versions of the dataset.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker sex/gender information is collected to impose a balance of at least 30/70% sex ratio among speakers. Speakers are disjoint between train/dev and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The goal of FLEURS is to enable speech technology in more languages and catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding. The dataset aims to catalyze research towards building massively multilingual speech and text representations, enabling progress towards building speech technologies for everyone, including speakers of low-resource languages.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Results are much better on the Western European group than on other groups like Sub-Saharan African or South Asian, which can be explained in part due to larger amounts of unlabeled data in WE languages. Most of the data seen during pre-training is from Western European and Eastern European languages. CMN, SEA, SSA and SA are geographical regions known for language diversity but with limited amounts of publicly available pre-training data.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: About 21.5% of sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. The dataset covers only the dev and devtest sets of FLoRes-101 (2009 sentences) since the test set is not publicly available. Performance gaps exist across geographical groups, with Western European languages performing significantly better than Sub-Saharan African and South Asian languages. CJK languages show steep degradation in retrieval performance due to tokenization mismatch between fine-tuning and pre-training regimes.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: FLEURS can be used for: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Speech-to-Text Translation, Speech-to-Speech Translation, Multilingual Speech-to-Speech Retrieval, and Multilingual Speech-to-Text Retrieval. It is especially suited to evaluate data-efficient multilingual pre-trained representations of speech and text in a few-shot learning scenario.
